questions: What is standing by the sea at the start?
What keeps rushing at the cliff?
segments.say: A hard cliff stands by the sea. Watch the waves rush at the cliff face, again and again. On its own the rock just stands there - tell your partner: what arrives to change it?

questions: How does a bit of rock become loose?
What carries the loose bit away?
segments.say: The waves loosen bits of rock. Follow the crack as the battering works on the cliff, watch the loose bit break off, then follow the current as it carries the bit away along the coast.

questions: What two movers do the wearing?
What happens on a calm day with no waves and no wind?
segments.say: Moving water and wind do the wearing. Watch the gust of wind wear at the rock and move the worn-off pebble. Say it with me: rocks do not crumble on their own - moving water and wind do the wearing.

questions: Step by step, how did the cliff get smaller?
Where is the loosened rock now?
segments.say: Put the whole story together: cliff, battering waves, a loosened chip, then the current and wind carrying it away. Trace it with your finger from the cliff to the pebble and name the mover at each step.

questions: What really does the wearing at a cliff?
What would you say to someone who thinks rocks crumble by themselves?
segments.say: Here is the trap, sprung on purpose: it is tempting to think the rock just crumbles by itself, because solid rock looks as if nothing could move it. Watch the scenes again: every change has a mover behind it. Now work through the worksheet in pairs, checking each answer against the trap section of your student notes. Last, the exit ticket - on your own, no talking - and remember: if you can name the movers, you have cracked today's lesson.
segments.watchFor: Rocks crumble on their own, with nothing doing the wearing. Listen for students who say exactly this when they explain the cliff. Send them back to the scenes: waves loosen, currents carry, and wind wears - there is always a mover.

subject: geography
title: Erosion: wind and water wear rock away
